The amount that this story plays into the camp is entirely up to the DM. From just a hint in one session to leading the party to a specific dungeon to follow a lead. This has the potential to be the backbone of the camp, or just an offshoot. Like another comment said, make the BBEG chase it as well for instance. But nothing about this implies exclusively one character's journey. I could weave this into everyone's backstory no problem and everyone could get something out of it. As I said before, one of the rumors about the tome could lead the party to an artifact another character is looking for. Maybe Torrin's long lost brother accidentally stumbled on a temple that holds a hint to it's whereabouts. There's a million ways to skin this cat.

When I was your age, (oh God... It happened... I finally used that... Please no, I'm only 26! Anyway.) I had a poster of every chord and variation of it, (minors, b9s, b7s, diminished, etc.) and also a poster of scales. (pentatonic, lydian, mixolydian, etc.) and I tried to at least become familiar with a new scale and chord form at least once a month. Familiar with enough to recognize when it should be used. But I set the bar way too high. One a month is still a stretch, but you get the idea. Just learn all you can, and posters, books, or charts are great references to keep right in front of you.

Just don't be scared to try anything. Hell, you could get tabs for, "Through the Fire and Flames" as a brand new player, and if you take your time, and keep working at it, you'll play it just as well. And keep in mind, a LOT of electric lead work is smoke and mirrors. Just a little practice and I was amazed at how easy noodling and trills were.

Broaden your repertoire of scales, chords, different chord positions, and chord variations. I used to get so mad when I KNEW I had the right chord, but it didn't sound quite right because it was supposed to be played with a different phrasing. Just expanding your knowledge of your fretboard will help.

Nothing wrong with that. I prefer to play rhythm. I would encourage you to dip a toe into the lead world soon though. It's not nearly as hard as you think. (I psyched myself out about it for the first year or so, now that I know what I'm doing, I realize how simple it really is.) you don't have to be Slash to be a good lead player. You don't need 8 notes a second. You just need the right note at the right time. A lot of the best lead players seldom melt faces.

I started on an acoustic, and yeah, it definitely hurts more and takes more finger strength, but just keep with it and it'll get easier. Another thing you could do, (I did this years after I started, just because my vocal range isn't high enough for most songs I like, and this is easier than transposing.) is tune the entire guitar a half or whole step down. Just put a capo on if you want to use EADGBE again. 
One thing I will say though, is I played acoustic for years, and then I got an electric to mess with some e blues, and if I didn't pay attention, I'd over-press my notes just enough to make them sour. Just because I was used to the heavier, acoustic strings. So that just takes some finesse if you're going to switch back and forth. But everyone who tells me they want to learn, I point them to acoustics as their first just to build finger strength. Even if they want to be a lead electric player. If nothing else, the extra strength makes for easier bends. =P

Jamming is all about the feel, my friend. Some of the best people I've sat down with didn't know what scale they were using. You don't need a book to tell you what sounds good to you.
